content: The p-value in the analysis of treatment-by-visit interaction was derived from a Wald test. This test assessed whether there was a significant difference between study arms in the number of sexual partners (defined as total male partners with whom participants engaged in oral or anal sex over a 12-week recall period) during the study period. These results, along with a description of the analysis, were obtained through correspondence with the study authors and were not included in the original publication. In the Kenya intermittent PrEP study, slight changes in the number of sexual partners over time were reported, but statistical significance was not assessed. In another study, the mean number of partners did not differ significantly between months 12–24 and months 3–9 following the initiation of the study drug in the delayed arm (IRR = 0.56). The iPrEx study reported increased condom use from baseline to follow-up in both the FTC-TDF and control arms, with no significant difference in condom use rates between study arms over time (p = 0.36). Similarly, the CDC safety study and Project PrEPare observed decreased unprotected sex over time, with no significant differences across study arms. The CDC safety study also found a reduction in the number of sexual partners over time, with no significant differences between study arms. Despite the growing body of literature, awareness of PrEP among men who have sex with men (MSM) remains limited globally. However, some studies suggest that awareness has increased since the release of the iPrEx results. Willingness to use PrEP varies widely across studies, with reported acceptance rates ranging from 40% to 70%. Barriers to PrEP use include concerns about effectiveness, side effects, cost, accessibility, mistrust of healthcare providers, stigma, and risk compensation. Facilitators of PrEP use include its perceived effectiveness and safety. Studies on PrEP adherence highlight the importance of client-centered counseling, daily reminders, and individualized routines. Barriers to adherence include changes in routine, side effects, stress, stigma, and contextual factors such as social life and conflicts with partners. Facilitators of adherence include receiving high-quality, non-judgmental healthcare and counseling as part of clinical trials. Preferences for PrEP dosing and administration vary. In Boston, 90% of MSM preferred daily PrEP over intermittent options, while in Thailand, daily oral PrEP or long-lasting injections were favored. In Kenya, intermittent dosing was preferred by some participants, though challenges with post-coital dosing were noted. Regarding dispensing sites, participants in studies from Peru, Kenya, and the U.S. preferred obtaining PrEP from healthcare providers, particularly primary healthcare centers. Studies on risk compensation associated with PrEP use found varying degrees of anticipated behavior changes. For example, a U.S.-based survey of MSM found that 75% anticipated no change in condom use while on PrEP, though 21% perceived themselves at lower risk of HIV infection from unprotected insertive anal sex, and 39% from receptive anal sex. Other studies reported significant reductions in condom use among some participants while on PrEP. For instance, 35% of MSM in a New York City study and 35% of respondents in a study from China indicated they were less likely to use condoms while taking PrEP. In a study of MSM in serodiscordant relationships, 26% reported being more likely to engage in unprotected sex.
